title: Yoga (revisited)
hook: a weather report for the mind: Vyasa's five grounds, from scattered to stilled

segments.voice: Yesterday Yoga laced up its boots: Samkhya's map, walked, with the mind given one thing to rest on. When your mind raced, did it settle at all? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-two.

A weather report never says the sky is good or bad. It says what's up there. Clear. Overcast. Gusts. Fog rolling in by evening. Nobody gets angry at the forecaster for mentioning the fog. It's just useful to know what you're walking into. The Yoga Sutras come down to us with a commentary attached, credited by tradition to a sage named Vyasa. And in his very first comment, before the work has properly begun, Vyasa gives a weather report for the mind. Five kinds of sky. Today we read it.
screen: `A WEATHER REPORT.` → `NO GOOD SKY, NO BAD SKY.` → `FIVE SKIES OF THE MIND.`

segments.voice: The first sutra only says that the teaching of yoga begins now. Vyasa opens his comment on it with a short line: yoga is samadhi. Samadhi is the settled, absorbed mind. Then he says something easy to miss. Samadhi, in some form, is a quality of the mind in every one of its grounds. And he names the grounds. Kshipta, the scattered mind, thrown in every direction. Mudha, the dull mind, heavy and fogged over. Vikshipta, the distracted mind, which does settle now and then, but keeps getting pulled away. Ekagra, the one-pointed mind, resting on a single thing. And niruddha, the stilled mind, where the turnings have quieted. Here's the honest part. Vyasa says the moments of steadiness in a distracted mind don't count as yoga yet, because the distraction swallows them. Yoga proper, for him, belongs to the one-pointed and the stilled. That sounds strict, and it is. But read it as a report, not a grade. The list doesn't sort people into good and bad. It describes skies, and one person can pass under several of them before lunch. Last week, Samkhya gave us the gunas, light, motion and weight. Some readers of Yoga hear the same three strands in these grounds: the restless one, the heavy one, the clear one. That's what makes Yoga a school and not just a set of exercises. It takes a map seriously enough to ask where you are on it, right now. In the middle of a busy day, that's a useful first question. Not, why can't I focus. Just, which sky is this?
screen: `YOGA IS SAMADHI.` · `FIVE GROUNDS OF THE MIND.` · `STEADY MOMENTS AREN'T ENOUGH YET.` · `A REPORT, NOT A GRADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the sky for two minutes. Sit, and let your breath settle. First, just check. Is the mind racing, heavy, or coming and going? Name it once, without arguing. Then pick one thing, the feel of your hands resting in your lap, and rest on it. When attention drifts, notice which sky pulled you away, and come back. No score. If you pray, you can rest on a name you pray with instead of the breath. The bell holds the time.
Yoga. In Vyasa's first comment, yoga is samadhi, and the mind has five grounds: scattered, dull, distracted, one-pointed and stilled.
Your line: Yoga, revisited. Today, once or twice, check the weather in your mind and name the sky: scattered, dull, distracted or one-pointed. Then carry on. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Students of Yoga philosophy read the Yoga Sutras together with Vyasa's commentary, and teachers often use his five grounds of the mind to help a student see where their attention is before they begin to practice.

match.prompt: Vyasa's grounds of the mind — tap the pairs.

myth: Vyasa's first comment says yoga is samadhi
his commentary opens: yoga is samadhi.
for Vyasa, the steady moments of a distracted mind already count as yoga
he says the distraction swallows them; yoga proper is the one-pointed and the stilled.
the five grounds sort people into good and bad
they describe states of the mind, and one person can pass through several in a day.

fork.setup: you sit down to practice, and the mind is foggy and heavy, like it hasn't woken up. in Vyasa's list, which ground is this?
fork.reveal: mudha. Vyasa names it without blame, the way a forecaster names fog. knowing the sky is where the practice starts.

original.note: Sanskrit: ground or level; the word used for the five grounds of the mind in Vyasa's commentary.

trapdoor: what you thought: yoga is something you do with your body.
what it means: in Vyasa's first comment, yoga is samadhi, a settled and absorbed mind.
what a scholar hears: Vyasa calls samadhi a quality of the mind in all its grounds, then reserves yoga proper for the one-pointed and the stilled.
recall: a saying: Akka Mahadevi's short free poems

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras 1.1 (now, the teaching of yoga)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.1 (yoga is samadhi; the five grounds: kshipta, mudha, vikshipta, ekagra, niruddha; distracted samadhi is not yoga)

notes: Bhashya on 1.1 paraphrase: 'yogah samadhih'; samadhi as a quality of the mind in all its grounds (sarvabhauma); the five chitta-bhumis; samadhi in the vikshipta mind is subordinate to distraction and not reckoned as yoga. Confirm wording.
Authorship of the Bhashya is given as 'credited by tradition to Vyasa'. Check the phrasing is acceptable.
The link between the grounds and the three gunas is attributed to some readers, not to Vyasa directly. Confirm, or cut that sentence.
'bhumi' as the original word: the compound chitta-bhumi is the usual later name; confirm Vyasa's own phrasing.
The five grounds were also touched in year two (day 439); this day frames them as Vyasa's opening move.
